cca.title: Canonical correspondence analysis (CCA)
cca.summary: 20 cases, 6 variables, total inertia 0.5697: 2 explanatory column(s) constrain 63.6% of it (adjusted 59.3%), pseudo-F = 14.823, p = 0.005 (199 permutations).
assumptions: CCA is correspondence analysis constrained by the explanatory variables: the axes are linear combinations of them, in the chi-square geometry — so it needs counts (or another non-negative measure on one common scale) and assumes unimodal responses along a gradient.
Sites carry their row masses: a site with more counts weighs more, in the fit and in every correlation reported here. That is what makes this CCA and not an RDA on transformed data.

Significance is by permutation (199 rearrangements, seed 5) — the explanatory block is shuffled, so each site keeps its own counts and its own mass: p = (r + 1) / (permutations + 1), and the smallest p reachable here is 0.005.
Each term is tested marginally — what it adds when entered last, with the variable residualised against the others before shuffling, so collinearity is respected.
Adjusted R2 (Ezekiel) is the one to report: R2 rises with every variable added, adjusted R2 does not.
Scaling "symmetric": both families scaled by the square root of the inertia — the usual choice when both are read together.
Per-axis permutation tests are not offered: testing the axes one after another has more than one convention, and they give different p-values, so only the whole model and each term are tested.
cca.cite: Canonical correspondence analysis (ter Braak 1986) of a 20 x 6 table constrained by 2 explanatory column(s); 199 permutations.

dbrda.title: Distance-based redundancy analysis (db-RDA)
dbrda.summary: 24 cases on the Bray-Curtis dissimilarity, constrained by 2 explanatory column(s): 76.2% of the variation is explained (adjusted 73.9%), pseudo-F = 33.580, p = 0.005 (199 permutations).
assumptions: db-RDA is RDA on principal coordinates: the Bray-Curtis dissimilarity is turned into coordinates first, then the axes are forced to be linear combinations of the explanatory variables. Use it when the distance you care about is not Euclidean.
Distance: Bray-Curtis.
Significance is by permutation (199 rearrangements, seed 5): p = (r + 1) / (permutations + 1), so the smallest p reachable here is 0.005.
Each term is tested marginally — what it adds when entered last, with the variable residualised against the others before shuffling, so collinearity is respected.
Adjusted R2 (Ezekiel) is the one to report: R2 rises with every variable added, adjusted R2 does not.

The variables are placed by weighted averaging (a variable sits at the centre of the cases it is abundant in). They are positions, not loadings — a distance matrix gives the columns no direction, so this method draws no variable arrows.
Per-axis permutation tests are not offered: testing the axes one after another has more than one convention, and they give different p-values, so only the whole model and each term are tested.
11 negative eigenvalue(s) (11.1% of the retained variation): the Bray-Curtis dissimilarity is not Euclidean, so those axes cannot be represented and are dropped before the regression.
dbrda.cite: Distance-based redundancy analysis (Legendre & Anderson 1999) on the Bray-Curtis dissimilarity of 24 cases; 199 permutations.

varpart.title: Variance partitioning
varpart.summary: 40 cases, 4 response variables, 3 blocks: together they explain 94.8% of the variation (adjusted), leaving 5.2% unexplained. The largest single fraction is [d] Climate ∩ Soil at 58.8%.
assumptions: Every fraction is an adjusted R² (Ezekiel): a raw R² rises with each column added, so raw fractions would reward the widest block rather than the most informative one.
The unique fractions are tested by partial redundancy analysis — that block with the other(s) held constant, 199 permutations, seed 4.
A shared fraction has no test and is reported without one: it is a difference between two models, not the fit of any model, so there is nothing to permute.

A shared fraction can come out negative. That is a real result, not an error: it means the blocks together explain less than the sum of their separate explanations, which happens when they are related to the response in opposing ways. 4 fraction(s) here are negative.
The fractions are shares of the total variation, so they sum with the residual to 1.
Linear (redundancy-analysis) geometry. This is not offered on correspondence analysis: the adjusted R² that makes the fractions comparable is not defined there.
varpart.cite: Variance partitioning (Borcard, Legendre & Drapeau 1992; adjusted R² after Peres-Neto et al. 2006) of 4 response variables over 3 blocks; 199 permutations.

meltingtemp.title: Melting temperature (Tm)
meltingtemp.summary: Melting temperature by sigmoid fit (flat baselines) and first derivative. Apo: Tm 52.2 °C; Ligand: Tm 56.15 °C.
assumptions: One two-state transition per curve inside the temperature window.
Both plateaus are flat.
Tm (fit) is the sigmoid's midpoint; Tm (derivative) is the steepest point of the smoothed curve. They agree for a symmetric transition.
A sample's Tm is the mean of its replicate columns; its SE is the fit SE for one column, SD/√n for several.
ΔTm's interval treats the sample and the control as independent (Welch–Satterthwaite degrees of freedom).
meltingtemp.cite: Two-state melting curve fitted with a Boltzmann sigmoid; Tm is its midpoint.
